title: Developing an Ecosystem of Service Providers: A Conversation with Tracey Yurko
pub: The Practice (Harvard Law School Center on the Legal Profession), March/April 2021 — 'Law Firm Responses to the Big Four' issue, Speaker's Corner
author: David B. Wilkins · Tracey Yurko

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Big Four: Integration matters more than replacement
st.an: Yurko accepts the integration-over-replacement framing and materially strengthens it with a concrete pilot in which an in-house department, law firm and PwC combined complementary roles while reducing costs by more than 50%. She also preserves law firms’ strategic role and treats any Big Four advantage as conditional on regulatory change.
qs: We were able to cut the cost by more than 50% by doing a collaboration.

We had the law firm providing the high-level strategic thinking and legal expertise to get a template for the work, which we then translated across multiple different fund structures, with support from PwC.

st.t: Partnership structure: AI tests governance beyond capital scarcity
st.an: Yurko accepts that adaptation depends on organizational capabilities beyond capital and concretely develops the cluster’s alternatives by identifying the Big Four’s conditional advantage in integrated legal services. She also adds a material governance constraint: auditor-independence rules may limit integration and require structural separation.
qs: **Yurko:** On balance, I have to give the advantage to the Big Four if (and for now that is an if) regulations change and allow them to practice law.
If they are your auditor, then there are limitations on what non-audit services they can provide to you.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source provides a concrete operational example of institutional absorption: Bridgewater phased pilots, selected repeatable work for technology or ALSP delivery, and reorganised lawyers’ time toward higher-value business advice. It also reinforces uneven adoption through variable law-firm participation, although its evidence concerns technology-enabled service delivery generally rather than AI specifically and remains qualitative.
qs: > As you make your way down from complex to more routine matters, we identified the repeatable things that could be technology enabled and what could be serviced by an alternative legal service provider.
My senior lawyers, for instance, are seeing their time freed up so that they’re able to spend more time partnering and problem solving with the business—highest and best use.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition and materially extends it with a concrete buyer-side operating model: Bridgewater segments repeatable, non-advisory work for technology-enabled delivery by PwC, pilots the model incrementally, and reports emerging capacity gains that redirect senior lawyers toward business partnering rather than replace them.
qs: > As you make your way down from complex to more routine matters, we identified the repeatable things that could be technology enabled and what could be serviced by an alternative legal service provider.
My senior lawyers, for instance, are seeing their time freed up so that they’re able to spend more time partnering and problem solving with the business—highest and best use.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not assess AI’s jagged capabilities or verification directly, but materially extends the cluster’s work-redesign thesis with a tested provider-allocation model. Its pilot divided strategic legal judgment from scalable implementation across a law firm, the client and PwC, reportedly reducing cost by more than 50%.
qs: We had the law firm providing the high-level strategic thinking and legal expertise to get a template for the work, which we then translated across multiple different fund structures, with support from PwC.
We were able to cut the cost by more than 50% by doing a collaboration.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Bridgewater’s account supports the cluster’s delivery-redesign and buyer-side adoption propositions. It describes phased process redesign that reallocates repeatable, non-advisory work to technology and an ALSP, freeing senior in-house lawyers for higher-value business work. The evidence is qualitative and does not address pricing, apprenticeship, verification or market-wide effects.
qs: > As you make your way down from complex to more routine matters, we identified the repeatable things that could be technology enabled and what could be serviced by an alternative legal service provider.
My senior lawyers, for instance, are seeing their time freed up so that they’re able to spend more time partnering and problem solving with the business—highest and best use.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: Yurko supports the cluster’s account of converging providers and business-model competition. She identifies the Big Four’s integrated, multidisciplinary services as a conditional advantage over narrower law-firm offerings, while noting that regulatory permission and audit-independence rules constrain that model. Her discussion of partnerships, acquisitions and funding also aligns with the cluster’s view that broader capabilities may require new capital structures, though she frames these as strategic questions rather than proven solutions.
qs: **Yurko:** On balance, I have to give the advantage to the Big Four if (and for now that is an if) regulations change and allow them to practice law.
They can deliver a more integrated type of service.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source supports buyer-led workflow unbundling and complementary delivery: Bridgewater explores ALSPs and lower-cost methods for suitable work while retaining law firms for complex, judgment-intensive advice. It also reinforces the cluster’s view that scale, financing and regulation shape which providers can deliver adjacent services.
qs: In this sense, partnerships between law firms (who can provide the legal advice) and the Big Four or other ALSPs could be equally important to both sides.
If there is a way for us to get a good work product in a really efficient way that also costs less—that’s something we have to consider and try to pursue.

kp.k: Technology and ALSP adoption serve four client objectives
kp.d: In this March/April 2021 interview, Yurko describes Bridgewater’s exploration of technology and alternative legal service providers as driven by innovation, access to appropriate legal technology, talent development and cost efficiency, rather than dissatisfaction with valued law firms. Her account concerns technology-enabled service delivery, not specific AI capabilities or measured AI effects.
qs: The question was how could we source legal tech, in partnership with our internal technology team, that would best enable our lawyers and regulatory professionals.
Our internal lawyers and regulatory professionals could then be freed up to spend more time focusing on becoming strategic thought partners to the business and advising on the most complex matters.
The final leg was about bending the cost curve.

kp.k: Work segmentation reallocates routine tasks and senior attention
kp.d: Yurko reports classifying work by complexity to identify repeatable activities suitable for technology enablement or ALSP delivery. Over the preceding approximately 18 months, Bridgewater had worked with PwC on technology and processes for work not constituting legal advice, progressing from small pilots toward expansion. She reports senior lawyers gaining time for business partnership, without quantifying the time released.
qs: In order to determine which work was ripe for technology enablement and ALSP services, we needed a taxonomy of the work and therefore classified it into levels.

Over the last 18 months or so, we’ve been actively working with PwC to tech enable some of our functions and build processes (or “machines” as we call them at Bridgewater) to leverage PwC talent for some of the work that doesn’t constitute legal advice.
My senior lawyers, for instance, are seeing their time freed up so that they’re able to spend more time partnering and problem solving with the business—highest and best use.

kp.k: One collaborative pilot cut costs by more than half
kp.d: Yurko describes a single pilot priced both as an entirely law-firm-delivered project and as a collaboration among Bridgewater, a law firm and PwC. She reports a cost reduction exceeding 50% through collaboration: the firm supplied strategic and legal expertise for a template, with PwC supporting its application across fund structures. This is a client-reported project outcome, not a market-wide estimate.
qs: For example, for one of the pilots we ran, we priced the project two ways: (1) for a law firm to do the whole project and (2) to have a law firm partner with us and PwC.
We were able to cut the cost by more than 50% by doing a collaboration.

We had the law firm providing the high-level strategic thinking and legal expertise to get a template for the work, which we then translated across multiple different fund structures, with support from PwC.

kp.k: Law firms respond through technology, collaboration and cheaper locations
kp.d: Yurko observes uneven adaptation among Bridgewater’s law firms: some global firms use technology to track regulatory shifts, some collaborate with PwC, firms accommodate client-selected e-discovery technology or offer established options, and some locate offices in lower-cost areas. These are observations about her providers rather than systematic evidence of sector-wide adoption.
qs: First, some of the firms we use that have a global presence have used technology to help us track regulatory shifts.
Another thing that we have seen is that some firms—not all—have had a willingness to partner with PwC and us on projects.
I have seen firms be willing to partner with a technology of our choosing and to have their own established options.
I’ve also seen some of the law firms that we use open offices in less expensive areas of the country so that they can provide certain types of service at a lower rate.

kp.k: Legal-practice restrictions constrain Big Four expansion
kp.d: Responding to Wilkins’s question about providers moving up the value chain, Yurko identifies the Big Four’s inability to practice law in the United States, as she describes it at the time, as a major barrier. She emphasizes the difficulty of distinguishing legal advice from other work and argues that partnerships with law firms can therefore benefit both sides. She also stresses the continuing importance of law firms’ complex advice.
qs: For us, it’s certainly been a very fine needle to thread to make sure that we’re distinguishing between what is and what isn’t giving legal advice.
The inability to practice law—and the complexities of determining where that line is—is going to be a real roadblock for the Big Four to move all the way up the value chain.
In this sense, partnerships between law firms (who can provide the legal advice) and the Big Four or other ALSPs could be equally important to both sides.

kp.k: Law firms retain expertise but face scaling constraints
kp.d: Yurko credits law firms with strategic and technical legal reputations and a current advantage in recruiting top legal talent. However, she questions whether even firms with 500 or more lawyers can internally build and scale adjacent services quickly enough to match the Big Four. She cites Ernst & Young’s acquisition of Pangea3, described in the interview as occurring “last year,” as an example of the Big Four’s existing positioning.
qs: Law firms also have deep experience and reputations for giving great strategic and technical legal advice, which the Big Four and other ALSPs don’t yet have.
And law firms have, at least for now, the edge on the ability to recruit the top legal talent.
Even a big law firm of 500 or more lawyers is not a huge company.
The Big Four are already suited to this type of business—Ernst & Young acquired Pangea3 last year, for example.
The speed and scale at which the Big Four can operate is just different than even the largest law firms.

kp.k: Regulatory liberalization could favor integrated Big Four services
kp.d: Wilkins frames parallel constraints: restrictions on Big Four legal practice and on outside investment in US law firms. Yurko conditionally predicts an advantage for the Big Four if regulations permit legal practice, citing business understanding and existing multidisciplinary services. Her position is a hypothetical competitive assessment, not an observed outcome of reform.
qs: By similar logic, at least in the United States, big law firms cannot have outside investment, and therefore they have to finance everything, roughly speaking, through the personal contributions of the partners.
On balance, I have to give the advantage to the Big Four if (and for now that is an if) regulations change and allow them to practice law.
They can deliver a more integrated type of service. For them, they just need to add the legal piece.
How do they build out and get credibility in other broader areas without strategic partnerships or acquisitions? And, then, how do they fund them?

kp.d: Yurko qualifies her assessment of Big Four advantages by noting that auditor independence limits non-audit services to audit clients. She speculates that further audit-market reform might eventually prompt service spin-offs; she does not report a decided restructuring.
qs: If they are your auditor, then there are limitations on what non-audit services they can provide to you.
These two things cannot always live happily together.
Because of this, perhaps in time and with further reform of the audit services market, we may see the Big Four spinning some services off as separate businesses.

kp.k: Provider evaluation combines outcome review and ongoing feedback
kp.d: Yurko says Bridgewater seeks evidence-based evaluation but has not solved how to measure legal practice. Its experiments include advice and risk metrics, investigation of bad outcomes, shared rating vocabulary and continuous feedback. Wilkins contrasts this with traditional firms’ reliance on input-based quality proxies. Yurko reports firms’ willingness to review outcomes, while remaining unsure whether any had requested participation in internal ratings.
qs: And, by the way, we have not cracked the nut yet in my department of how you do this when it comes to the practice of law.
We do track some metrics on advice and risk, and we’ve been able to lean on some of the tools that we use as a company.
The idea is that we have a rating system and it’s a constant feedback loop.

The big challenge for traditional law firms is that we have traditionally only had input-based measures of quality, which is to say, mostly, the quality is because of the people who did it, and we look very little at outcomes.
I’m not sure if any have asked, but our firms have been willing to participate in working through outcomes and seeing how we can improve in the future.

kp.k: Complexity-based spending preserves premiums for strategic work
kp.d: Yurko explains that the work taxonomy supports tracking expenditure separately for highly complex strategic work and lower-complexity work. Bridgewater remains willing to pay premium prices for the former while seeking greater efficiency for the latter; the interview does not specify a move to a particular billing model.
qs: And second, going back to what we were talking about earlier, the taxonomy work enables us to track how much we are paying for the most complex strategic work and how much we are paying for the lower complexity work.
We’re willing to pay that top dollar for the high complexity work, but the taxonomy lets us get the best bang for our buck on the lower complexity work.

kp.k: The virtual law firm balances integration and provider diversity
kp.d: Wilkins frames the GC as coordinating segmentation and integration across providers. Yurko advocates a business-oriented ecosystem combining internal teams, law firms, Big Four capabilities and technology partners. Her proposed “virtual law firm” treats external partners as team members while balancing deep company knowledge against excessive dependence on any one provider. She presents this as an evolving model whose optimal composition may change over 10 years.
qs: The GC is the person who tries to figure out how to segment work, who to segment it to, and then how to put these pieces together.
If you’re our outside partner, you’re part of our team.
You can’t have too many partners because then no one’s really going to know you well enough to understand you. But you also can’t have so few that you are overly reliant on any one.
And so, we sort of toyed with this, and we came up with the concept of the virtual law firm.
Moreover, what works in the short term might not look like what works in 10 years.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source makes no explicit AI-specific claims. Tracey Yurko describes technology enablement and ALSP collaboration as ways to redistribute legal-department work, free senior lawyers for strategic advice, and reduce costs.
pts.d: Yurko predicts that technology will become increasingly important in legal services, but does not identify AI as the technology involved. She reports that Bridgewater classified work by complexity, identified repeatable activities suitable for technology or ALSP delivery, and collaborated with PwC on functions and work that did not constitute legal advice. She says senior lawyers were beginning to gain time for business partnering and problem-solving. In one pilot, collaboration between Bridgewater, a law firm and PwC reportedly reduced costs by more than 50% relative to having the law firm perform the entire project. These are claims about technology and service-delivery organisation, not evidence of AI-driven automation or AI replacing lawyers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of Yurko’s first-hand account as Bridgewater’s chief legal officer, including a single pilot cost comparison; no AI evidence is offered.
pts.d: Yurko describes work classification, initial pilots, subsequent expansion of the PwC partnership, and observed changes in senior lawyers’ time allocation. The quantified cost claim concerns a project priced under two delivery models: law-firm-only delivery versus collaboration with Bridgewater and PwC. The law firm supplied strategic thinking, legal expertise and a template, which was then translated across fund structures with PwC support. The interview does not provide underlying cost data, a quantified measure of time freed, or an AI-specific contribution to the reported results. Yurko also acknowledges that her department has not resolved how to measure the quality of legal practice.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Reported operational changes concern approximately the 18 months preceding the March/April 2021 interview; future technology expectations are open-ended and constrained by work type and legal-practice boundaries.
pts.d: Yurko presents the partnership as new, cautiously piloted and only beginning to pay off at the time of publication. Technology enablement and ALSP delivery concern suitable repeatable or lower-complexity work, while law firms retain strategic legal expertise. She identifies the Big Four’s inability to practise law in the United States, as she describes the position in 2021, as a barrier to moving fully up the value chain. Her separate prediction that the Big Four could gain a competitive advantage through integrated services is expressly conditional on regulatory change, not on AI capabilities. She supplies no AI adoption or displacement timeline.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The described effects concern an enterprise legal buyer, its in-house lawyers and regulatory professionals, and its outside law firms, PwC and technology providers—not AI-specific labour displacement or public access to justice.
pts.d: For Bridgewater, the intended benefits are more efficient spending and more strategically focused legal support. In-house lawyers and regulatory professionals are intended to spend less time on work suitable for technology enablement or external delivery. Outside law firms contribute complex advice and legal templates; PwC supports appropriate non-advice work and processes. Yurko envisages a 'virtual law firm' combining complementary providers, while balancing familiarity with the client against overdependence on any one provider. These are enterprise service-delivery and role-allocation claims; she does not claim reduced lawyer headcount or effects on unmet civil legal need.
